title: Ad Click Aggregator
prompt: Design a system that counts clicks on ads, per ad per minute, for an ad network with billions of clicks a day. Advertisers watch the numbers live, and the same numbers are used to bill them.

clarify.q: Are these numbers used for billing, or only for dashboards?
clarify.why: Billing means no double counting and no loss, with an audit trail. Dashboards alone could tolerate approximate counts and a simpler pipeline.

clarify.q: Which time counts: when the click happened or when we received it?
clarify.why: Event time is correct for billing but forces us to handle out-of-order and late events with watermarks. Processing time is easy but wrong when a mobile client uploads hours later.

clarify.q: How late can a click arrive and still count?
clarify.why: Allowed lateness sets how long windows stay open, how much state we hold, and how many late events go to a correction path instead.

clarify.q: How fresh must the dashboard be?
clarify.why: About a minute lets us emit per-minute windows from a stream. Seconds would need smaller windows or an approximate live counter.

clarify.q: Which dimensions do advertisers slice by: country, device, campaign?
clarify.why: Each dimension multiplies the number of aggregate rows. That decides whether we pre-aggregate every combination or store finer rows in an OLAP store.

clarify.q: Do we filter duplicate and fraudulent clicks before counting?
clarify.why: Dedup by click ID needs state keyed by click. Fraud scoring may arrive later than the click, which means counts must be correctable after the fact.

functional: Record every ad click with ad ID, campaign, click ID, event time and a few dimensions (country, device).
Expose click counts per ad per minute, plus hourly and daily rollups, filterable by dimension.
Count each click at most once: duplicates from retries or double-taps are dropped by click ID.
Late clicks (up to 24 h) are still counted in the minute they happened.
Produce daily billing totals per campaign that match the raw click log.
nonFunctional: Ingest 2 B clicks/day with peaks of ~116 k/s, without dropping events.
Dashboard numbers no more than ~2 minutes behind real time.
Billing numbers exact after reconciliation (difference from raw log under 0.01%).
Click redirect latency unaffected by the counting pipeline (logging is async, p99 added under 5 ms).
Raw clicks kept 90 days for audits and replays.
outOfScope: Ad serving, auctions and impression tracking.
The fraud-detection model itself (we consume its verdicts).
Advertiser account management and invoicing UI.

assumptions: 2 B clicks per day; peak 5× average (big live events)
5 M active ads; ~400 k distinct ads get at least one click in a given minute
Aggregate row ≈ 40 bytes (ad, minute, count, dims hash)
Dedup window of 1 hour, ≈ 40 bytes of state per click ID

steps.label: Ingest bandwidth
steps.result: Small for a log: a few dozen partitions

steps.label: Raw log storage
steps.result: ≈ 54 TB raw, ≈ 11 TB as compressed columnar files (~5×)

steps.label: Aggregate rows
steps.math: 400 k ads × 1 440 minutes = 576 M rows/day; × 40 B
steps.result: ≈ 23 GB/day of per-minute rows before dimensions

steps.label: Sink writes
steps.math: 400 k rows each minute / 60 s ≈ 6.7 k rows/s
steps.result: ≈ 6.7 k upserts/s if flushes are spread out

steps.label: Dedup state
steps.result: ≈ 3.3 GB across all workers: fits in local state stores

estimates.takeaway:
The raw stream is modest in bytes (35 MB/s at peak), so the log is not the problem. The hard parts are correctness: event-time windows with late data, counting each click once across crashes and replays, and proving the billed number matches the raw log.

Aggregation turns 2 B events into ~576 M rows a day. That is only ~3.5× fewer in total, because an active ad averages only ~3.5 clicks a minute (1.39 M clicks / 400 k ads). The real win is per query: a day of one ad is at most 1 440 rows, however many clicks it had. The dashboard reads those rows, never the raw stream. One live ad can take a large share of the peak, so hot keys matter more than total volume.

api.note: Click redirect. The token is signed and carries adId, impressionId and a click ID. Logging is fire-and-forget to a local agent so the redirect never waits on the pipeline.

api.body: { clickId, adId, campaignId, eventTime, receivedAt, country, device, ipHash }
api.returns: consumed by the stream job and the archiver
api.note: Keyed by adId so one ad's clicks are in one partition, in order of arrival.
final=false while a minute is still inside the lateness window and may change.
Billing reads reconciled numbers once the daily batch has run.
Lets us subtract clicks found to be fraud after they were counted.

entities.name: Raw click
entities.store: Log topic (7 days) and object storage as Parquet (90 days), partitioned by event hour
entities.why: Immutable source of truth. Everything else can be recomputed from it, which is what makes reconciliation and replays possible.

entities.name: Minute aggregate
entities.store: OLAP column store (ClickHouse/Druid style) or Cassandra
fields: stream checkpoint or batch run ID
entities.why: Upsert by (adId, minute, dims) with absolute counts makes the sink idempotent: writing the same window twice gives the same row.

entities.name: Daily billing total
entities.why: Small, transactional, audited. Invoices are generated only from reconciled rows.

entities.name: Dedup state
entities.why: Drops retried and double-tapped clicks before counting. Checkpointed with input offsets so it survives restarts consistently.

data.note:
This is a CQRS split. The write model is an append-only click log, and the read model is a set of pre-aggregated tables shaped for the dashboard and billing queries. The aggregate store is partitioned by adId and sorted by minute, so a dashboard query for one ad over a day is a single range scan of 1 440 rows.

Hourly and daily rollups are computed from minute rows by the store's materialized views or a small job.

hld.summary:
The click redirect service validates the signed token, redirects the user immediately, and hands the event to a local agent that batches it to the clicks.raw log. Two consumers read the log. An archiver writes hourly Parquet files to object storage. A stateful stream job deduplicates by click ID, assigns each click to a one-minute event-time window, and emits per-(ad, minute, dims) counts when the watermark passes the window end. It emits updated counts for late clicks within the allowed lateness.

Counts are upserted into an OLAP store that serves dashboards. Every night, a batch job recomputes the previous day from the raw Parquet files, minus fraud verdicts, and compares it with the streaming numbers. It overwrites them and writes reconciled billing totals. The stream is fast and nearly right; the batch is slow and authoritative.

diagram.title: Streaming path and batch reconciliation
diagram.src:
flowchart LR

  R --> AG[Local log agent]
  AG --> K["clicks.raw topic"]
  K --> SJ["Stream job: dedup, windows"]
  FR[Fraud service] --> INV["clicks.invalidated topic"]
  INV --> SJ
  SJ --> OL[(OLAP aggregates)]
  K --> AR[Archiver]
  AR --> S3["Object storage (Parquet)"]
  S3 --> BJ[Nightly batch job]
  BJ --> OL
  BJ --> BILL[(Billing totals)]
  OL --> API[Query API]
  API --> D[Advertiser dashboard]

flows.title: A click is counted
steps: Redirect service verifies the token signature and expiry, responds 302, and writes the event to the local agent's buffer.
Agent batches events and produces them to clicks.raw keyed by adId, with idempotent producer retries.
Stream job drops the click if its clickId was seen in the last hour, otherwise adds it to the (adId, minute, dims) window.
When the watermark passes minute end + 30 s, the window fires and the job upserts the absolute count to the OLAP store.
Dashboard queries read minute rows; rows still inside the lateness window are flagged final=false.

flows.title: A click arrives 20 minutes late
steps: Its event time falls in a window that has already fired.
Because it is within the allowed lateness (1 h), the job updates that window's state and re-emits the new absolute count.
The upsert overwrites the old row; the dashboard number for that minute rises by one.
Clicks later than 1 h go to a late-events side topic; the nightly batch counts them correctly.

flows.title: Nightly reconciliation
steps: Batch job reads yesterday's Parquet partitions plus late files, dedups by clickId, and subtracts invalidated clicks.
It computes per-ad per-minute counts and per-campaign daily totals.
It compares with the streaming rows; any campaign differing by more than 0.1% raises an alert for investigation.
It overwrites the day's aggregate rows with batch values (version = runId) and writes reconciled billing totals.

deepDives.title: Windows, watermarks and late events
deepDives.problem: Clicks arrive out of order. Phones batch them, regions lag, and a client offline on a plane uploads hours later. If we count by arrival time, a minute's number depends on network luck. If we count by event time, we have to decide when a minute is 'done', because one more click could still arrive.

options.name: Processing-time windows
options.how: Bucket each click by when the stream job sees it.
pros: Windows close on a timer; no waiting
Minimal state
cons: Counts shift into the wrong minute whenever there is lag
A replay after an outage puts hours of clicks into one minute

options.name: Event-time windows with a watermark
options.how: Bucket by eventTime. A watermark (roughly max event time seen minus 30 s of expected disorder) says 'no older events are expected now'. A window fires when the watermark passes its end.
pros: Counts land in the minute the click happened, even after replays
Deterministic: the same input gives the same output
cons: Emits ~30 s after minute end
A stalled partition holds back the watermark for the whole job unless idle partitions are handled

options.name: Event-time plus allowed lateness and a side output
options.how: After the window fires, keep its state for 1 h more; late clicks update it and re-emit. Anything later goes to a side topic for batch to handle.
pros: Most late data still corrects the live numbers
Bounded state: windows are dropped after 1 h
cons: Downstream must accept updates to already-emitted rows
Needs a correction path for very late data

deepDives.choice:
Event-time tumbling one-minute windows, with a 30 s bounded-disorder watermark, 1 h allowed lateness, and a side output for anything later. Each emission is the absolute count for that key, so re-emits are plain overwrites. The dashboard shows final=false for minutes still within the lateness horizon.

Event time comes from the signed token, never from the client's clock alone, so nobody can backdate clicks. If most traffic were from devices that upload in daily batches, I would widen lateness only on that source, or rely more on batch.

deepDives.title: Counting each click exactly once
deepDives.problem: Workers crash, the log redelivers, producers retry, and users double-tap. Billing must neither double count nor lose clicks. 'Exactly once' has to hold end to end: from the log, through the job's state, into the aggregate store.

options.name: At-least-once plus increment sink
options.how: Consume, add +N to the sink row, and commit offsets afterwards.
pros: Simplest; works with any store that has counters
cons: Any replay after a crash adds the same clicks again
Overcounting cannot be detected without the raw log

options.name: Checkpointed state plus idempotent absolute upserts
options.how: The job periodically snapshots its state together with the input offsets. On failure it restores the last snapshot and replays from those offsets. Output rows carry absolute counts keyed by (adId, minute, dims), so re-writing them is harmless.
pros: No two-phase commit with the sink
Replays converge on the same values
Works with any key-value or OLAP store that supports upserts
cons: Between a crash and recovery, the sink may briefly show values from beyond the checkpoint, which are then rewritten with the same or corrected values
Sink must support upsert by key

options.name: Transactional sink (two-phase commit)
options.how: Output is written in a transaction that commits only when the checkpoint completes, such as a transactional log topic or a database transaction that also stores offsets.
pros: Readers never see uncommitted output
Works even when output is a delta
cons: Output is delayed until each checkpoint completes (e.g. every 30 s)
Needs a sink that supports transactions; harder to operate

deepDives.choice:
Checkpointed state plus idempotent absolute upserts. Combined with dedup by clickId inside the checkpointed state, a click is counted once even if the job restarts mid-minute. That also covers double taps and agent retries.

The mistake to call out is writing increments: they make replays add up. If the sink only supported counters, or we published aggregates to another topic for downstream jobs, I would use a transactional sink instead and accept the checkpoint-interval delay.

diagram.title: Crash and replay with idempotent upserts
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant K as Click log
  participant J as Stream job
  participant CK as Checkpoint store
  participant O as OLAP store
  J->>CK: snapshot state and offset 5000
  K->>J: clicks 5001 to 5400
  J->>O: upsert ad 7, 12:01, count 812
  Note over J: worker crashes
  J->>CK: restore state at offset 5000
  K->>J: replay clicks 5001 to 5400
  J->>O: upsert ad 7, 12:01, count 812 again
  Note over O: same row, same value

deepDives.title: Lambda, Kappa and reconciliation
deepDives.problem: The stream is fast but has known gaps. Very late clicks, fraud verdicts that arrive hours later, and bugs in the job code all make it drift. Billing needs a number we can defend in an audit. Do we run two pipelines, or one?

options.name: Lambda: separate batch and speed layers
options.how: A batch layer recomputes everything from raw data; a speed layer covers only recent hours; the serving layer merges them.
pros: Batch is the trusted source of truth
Batch can use slow but exact logic (fraud joins, full dedup)
cons: Same logic written twice, which drifts over time
Merging two views at query time is complex

options.name: Kappa: stream only, replay to fix
options.how: One streaming job. To fix a bug, deploy a new version that replays the log from an old offset into a new table, then switch.
pros: One codebase
Reprocessing uses the same code that runs live
cons: Needs long retention in the log, or the ability to replay from object storage
Replaying days of data through a stateful job is slow and costly

options.name: Kappa for serving plus batch reconciliation
options.how: Stream serves all live numbers. A nightly batch job recomputes closed days from the raw archive, compares, alerts on drift, and overwrites the day with authoritative values.
pros: Dashboards stay simple: one table
Billing gets an exact number with an audit trail
Drift between the two is itself a monitoring signal
cons: Counting logic still exists twice, so share it as one library
Numbers for yesterday can change once, after the batch run

deepDives.choice:
Kappa for serving plus batch reconciliation. I keep the core counting logic (dedup rule, window assignment, invalid-click rule) in one shared library used by both the stream and batch jobs. That shrinks Lambda's two-codebases problem to one function.

Invoices read only reconciled rows. A drift above 0.1% pages someone, because it usually means a bug, not lateness. If the business were dashboards only, I would drop the batch job and rely on replay. If fraud verdicts routinely arrived days later, I would reconcile again at day 7.

deepDives.title: Hot ads and skewed partitions
deepDives.problem: Keying by adId keeps an ad's clicks together, which windowing needs. But a single ad during a live sports final can get 30 k clicks/s, about a quarter of our peak, all on one partition and one worker. That worker falls behind and holds back the watermark for everyone.

options.name: Bigger machines
options.how: Scale the whole job vertically so the hottest worker keeps up.
pros: No code change
cons: Every other worker is over-provisioned
There is always a hotter ad

options.name: Two-stage aggregation with salting
options.how: Stage 1 keys by (adId, minute, salt 0..N-1) with a random salt and pre-aggregates. Stage 2 re-keys by (adId, minute) and sums N partial counts.
pros: Hot ad's load spreads over N workers
Stage 2 handles only N small partial counts per window
cons: Extra shuffle and a few seconds more latency
Dedup must happen before salting (keyed by clickId), or the same click could land in two salts

options.name: Local pre-aggregation before the shuffle
options.how: Each worker combines counts per key in memory for ~1 s before sending them on.
pros: Cuts shuffle volume by orders of magnitude for hot keys
No change to key layout
cons: Adds up to ~1 s of latency
Does not help if the downstream keyed worker is itself the bottleneck

deepDives.choice:
Dedup first, keyed by clickId, which spreads evenly. Then local pre-aggregation, then a keyed stage by (adId, minute). Salting applies only to ads flagged hot, detected when a key's rate passes ~5 k/s in the previous minute. Most ads see a few clicks a minute and do not need it.

To keep one slow partition from freezing every window, the watermark marks partitions idle after ~1 minute without data. If skew became the norm rather than the exception, I would salt every key and always run the two-stage path.

failures: Restart from the last checkpoint and replay from its offsets; absolute upserts make the replayed rows identical. Dashboard lags for a minute or two.
Log agent on a redirect host cannot reach the cluster
Agent buffers to local disk for hours; idempotent producer and clickId dedup make later delivery safe. The redirect itself is never blocked.
Stream job back-pressures and stops reading; the log retains 7 days, so nothing is lost. Catch up after recovery.
A bug overcounts for six hours
Reconciliation flags drift; deploy the fix and replay those hours into a new table version, or let the nightly batch overwrite the day.
Fraud service declares 10% of yesterday's clicks invalid
Invalidation events reduce live counts; billing uses the reconciled totals, which subtract them. Invoices are never sent from provisional numbers.
One partition stalls and the watermark stops
Idle-partition detection advances the watermark; alert on per-partition lag so the stall is fixed, not hidden.
scale: 10× clicks (20 B/day): peak ~1.2 M/s and ~350 MB/s. Add partitions and job parallelism; dedup state grows to ~33 GB, still fine in local state across workers.

Add impressions (~100× clicks): exact dedup per impression gets expensive. Count impressions with sampling or approximate distinct counts for dashboards, and compute exact numbers in batch only where billing needs them.
More dimensions: do not pre-aggregate every combination. Store minute rows with a few dimensions in a column store and let it aggregate at query time.

followups.q: How do you stop someone from replaying the same click token 1 000 times?
answer: The token carries a unique clickId signed with the impression; dedup drops repeats within the 1 h window.
Tokens expire (e.g. 1 h after the impression), so old tokens are rejected at the redirect.
Burst patterns per IP or device feed the fraud service, which invalidates clicks after the fact.

followups.q: Why not just use a database counter per ad per minute?
answer: ~116 k increments/s at peak, concentrated on a few hot rows, would lock-contend.
Increments are not idempotent, so any retry double counts.
There is no event-time handling or audit trail.

followups.q: How does an advertiser see a number that is a few seconds fresh?
answer: Show the last fired minutes from the OLAP store, plus an in-progress estimate for the current minute.
The in-progress number comes from the job's pre-window counts published every few seconds to a cache.
Label it as provisional; billing never reads it.

followups.q: How would you change the allowed lateness from 1 h to 24 h?
answer: Window state grows 24× in time; at ~400 k active keys per minute that is 576 M window states, too many to keep live.
Instead keep 1 h live and route later events to the side topic for an hourly mini-batch correction job.
Or make the late path a second, cheaper stream job that only updates already-closed windows.
Consumer lag in seconds per partition, and watermark delay vs wall clock.
Late-event rate, since a jump means a client or region problem.
Stream vs batch drift per campaign above 0.1%.

mistakes: Counting by processing time, so a backlog after an outage piles into the wrong minutes.
Writing increments to the sink and calling the system exactly-once.
No plan for clicks that arrive after their window closed.
Billing straight from the streaming numbers with no reconciliation against the raw log.
Keying everything by adId and never considering one ad taking a quarter of the traffic.
